# ARC demonstration-driven rule inference

Use for ARC tasks where a test grid is accompanied by one or more demonstrations. Infer a transformation that generalizes, rather than matching a visual hunch.

## Procedure

1. **Parse the full instance.** Record dimensions, distinct colors, repeated backgrounds, exceptional shapes/markers, and any action/attempt/demo caps. Keep row/column coordinates explicit and use them consistently.
2. **Compare each demo cell-by-cell.** Align input and output at matching coordinates when dimensions match. List changed coordinates and their before/after colors; separately note additions, removals, recolorings, dimension changes, and preserved seed structures. If dimensions differ, identify segmentation or object-count mappings that explain the change.
3. **Form a small set of competing rules.** Consider geometry, relative position, orientation, counts, symmetry, lines/regions, and transparency. Do not infer an anchor, target color, or direction solely from visual resemblance.
4. **Replay candidates on the demo.** Apply each candidate to the full demo input and compare every output cell and dimension exactly. Reject rules that leave changes unexplained or predict changes in preserved cells. All demos should fit one rule, aside from supported parameter changes such as color or size.
5. **Use demonstrations economically.** A demo request has a cost. Request one only when a specific unresolved ambiguity could materially change the test output. First extract all constraints from existing examples and test concrete hypotheses; do not request merely because the rule is not immediately obvious.
6. **Apply the validated rule to the test.** Preserve unrelated cells unless demonstrations show otherwise. Verify bounds, row and column counts, allowed values, and output dimensions before submission.

This task family has varied grid sizes and palettes; each demo output is same dimensions and differs by recoloring a localized connected object/component, while many other objects and even same-color components stay untouched. Never use global palette substitution or infer a fixed target/replacement color. Observed demo changes (1-indexed): pair 1, a 3-cell color-4 object at rows 2-3, cols 24-25 becomes 9; pair 2, a 4-cell color-9 object at rows 5-7, cols 19-20 becomes 0; pair 3, one color-8 cell at row 25, col 12 becomes 9; pair 4, a vertical three-cell color-4 object at rows 19-21, col 4 becomes 1; pair 5, three adjacent color-9 cells at row 5, cols 2-4 become 8; pair 6, the connected color-9 object around rows 6-11, cols 7-10 becomes 0; pair 7, the isolated color-0 cell at row 4, col 15 becomes 2; pair 8, the small color-5 component at rows 9-12, cols 16-17 becomes 8. The common selector/replacement mechanism was not identified from these examples; these local recolorings do not establish a simple color, size, edge, or line-alignment rule. Use local underlying structure and exact changed/preserved audit; validate every cell of the proposed output. Preserve connected/block-shaped objects such as the 1 regions and 8 forms.

A distinct instance had a full-height divider column (color 2) separating 10×27 and 10×27 panels; another demo had a full-width divider row (color 9) separating two 5×14 panels. This instance is a split-panel non-background occupancy overlap, confirmed by its demo: full vertical separator divides two equal-width panels; output is panel-sized, with 2 iff both aligned cells are nonzero, else 0. Infer stripe orientation and period from this instance's demos; task ID and prior diagonal cases do not fix either. Demos in this run: (1) 7x7 input had full rows `[0,7,6,6,3,2,4]`; output `[4,7,6,6,3,2,4]`, consistent with period 6 and sequence `[4,7,6,6,3,2]`. (2) Sparse down-right diagonal 9s produced a uniform 9 grid; treat as instance-specific and not evidence to fill unknown residues with 9 in another run. (3) 21x21 sparse horizontal rows 2,8,4,0,0,0,2,0,...,7,...,4,...,4,2 became the repeated period-8 sequence `[2,8,4,4,2,7,2,4]`. Accepted 4x4 test rows `[0,4,4,6]` became `[6,4,4,6]`, consistent with period 3 sequence `[6,4,4]`. Preserve phase and fill/correct rows according to the demo-derived repeat. Determine a period valid against every clue, replay demos, and do not assume a period from task ID or transfer the separate diagonal-residue rule's uncertain missing-class guesses.

## Confirmed recurring case: task-5c4cb9ae (18x18 to 6x6 mini-grid)
Partition the input into a regular grid of 3x3 tiles (not 6x6 tiles). Emit one output cell per tile, preserving tile row/column order. For each tile, ignore background/noise colors 0 and 5; if any other color is present, output that color, otherwise output 0. The demonstrated/test instance had a sole color-4 motif confined to the top-left 6x6 region: it landed in output tile row 0, column 1, producing [[0,4,0,0,0,0], then five all-zero rows]. This was accepted. An initial wrong attempt used 6x6 tiles and produced a 3x3 grid, so carefully distinguish tile size from output dimensions: 18x18 becomes 6x6 via 3x3 tiles. Validate all tile cells, including multi-color exceptional cells if present; the known instance only had color 4 among colors other than 0/5.

## Verified recurring case: task-a613028a (3x2 mirror tiling)
This task family expands any HxW input into a 3H x 2W output by mirror-tiling the original grid. For the demo 3x13 -> 9x26, each source row is expanded horizontally as `reverse(row) + row`; vertically the rows follow `[r3,r2,r1, r1,r2,r3, r3,r2,r1]`. This corresponds to three alternating mirrored row blocks.
